name: CONSORT 2025 statement (reporting randomised trials)
citation: Hopewell S, Chan A-W, Collins GS, Hrobjartsson A, Moher D, Schulz KF, et al. CONSORT 2025 statement: updated guideline for reporting randomised trials. BMJ 2025;389:e081123. Published simultaneously in JAMA, Lancet, Nat Med and PLOS Med (2025). The 30 numbered items keep the checklist's numbering; sub-items (1a/1b, 5a/5b, 12a/12b, 16a/16b, 17a/17b, 20a/20b, 21a-21d, 22a/22b, 23a/23b, 24a/24b) are folded into their item. See https://www.consort-spirit.org

items.question: Does the title say the study is a randomised trial, and does a structured abstract summarise its design, methods, results and conclusions?
Are the trial's registry, its registration number (with a link) and the date it was registered given?
Does the report say where the trial protocol and the statistical analysis plan can be read?
Does the report say whether, where and how de-identified participant data, analysis code and other trial materials can be obtained?
Are funding sources and other support named with the funders' role, and are the authors' financial and other conflicts of interest declared?
Is the scientific background explained and the reason for running this trial argued?
Are the trial's specific objectives stated, covering both the benefits and the harms it set out to assess?
Does the report say how patients or members of the public took part in designing, running or reporting the trial, or that they did not?
Is the design described: its type (e.g. parallel or crossover), the allocation ratio and the framework (superiority, equivalence, non-inferiority, exploratory)?
Are important changes made after the trial started reported with reasons, including outcomes or analyses that were not pre-specified?
Are the settings and the locations (countries, sites) where the trial ran described?
Are the participants' eligibility criteria given and, where relevant, those for the sites and for the people who delivered the interventions?
Are the intervention and the comparator described in enough detail for someone else to replicate them, including how and when they were given?
Are the pre-specified primary and secondary outcomes defined, each with its measurement variable, analysis metric, aggregation method and time point?

items.topic: How harms were defined and assessed
items.question: Does the report say how harms were defined and how they were assessed?
Is the way the sample size was determined explained with all its assumptions, and are any interim analyses and stopping rules described?
Does the report say who generated the allocation sequence and how, and which type of randomisation and restrictions (strata, blocks, block size) were used?
Is the mechanism that kept the allocation sequence concealed until assignment described, with the steps taken to conceal it?
Does the report say whether those who enrolled participants and those who assigned them to groups could see the allocation sequence?
Does the report say who was blinded after assignment and, if anyone was, how blinding was achieved and how similar the interventions were?
Are the group comparisons for every outcome described, with who each analysis includes, how missing data were handled and which extra analyses were pre-specified?
Does a flow diagram give, per group, the numbers randomised, given the intended intervention and analysed for the primary outcome, with losses and exclusions and reasons?
Are the dates of the recruitment and follow-up periods given and, if the trial ended or was stopped early, the reason?
Is it reported how the intervention and comparator were actually delivered, and what concomitant care each group received?
Is there a table of the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of each group?
For each outcome, are the numbers analysed per group, each group's result and the effect estimate with its precision given (absolute and relative for binary outcomes)?
Are all harms or unintended events reported for each group?
Are any other analyses, such as subgroup or sensitivity analyses, reported and labelled as pre-specified or post hoc?
Is the interpretation consistent with the results, weighing benefits against harms and setting them against other relevant evidence?
Are the trial's limitations discussed: sources of possible bias, imprecision, generalisability and, where relevant, the multiplicity of analyses?
